en_title: What Every Small Business Owner Needs to Learn to Grow Their Business. Why understanding every area of the company can be the difference between growing and closing your doors?
en_excerpt: When you run a small business, doing everything yourself is normal. Here are nine areas worth mastering so your business can grow with confidence.
en_meta_description: A practical guide for small business owners: financial control, pricing, sales, marketing and more to grow with confidence.
en_content:

Starting a business is, for many people, the fulfilment of a dream. The possibility of turning a skill, a passion or a market need into income leads thousands of people to start small businesses every year. However, there is a reality that is rarely shown on social media: at the beginning, the entrepreneur has to learn to perform several roles at the same time.

Before being able to hire specialised professionals or build a team, it is common for the entrepreneur to be the finance person, the salesperson, the one in charge of marketing and purchasing, the customer service contact and even the one who solves everyday problems.

Although it is challenging, understanding the basics of each area is not just a necessity — it is a strategy for the survival and growth of the business.

According to Michael Gerber (2001), many small businesses fail because the entrepreneur masters only the technical side of the service or product, but never learns to manage the company as a system. In other words, knowing how to do something well does not necessarily mean knowing how to run a business.

1. Financial Control: Without Numbers, There Is No Management

One of the greatest difficulties for small entrepreneurs lies in financial management.

Controlling income, outgoings, profits, expenses and cash flow is essential for the health of the company. Many businesses close not because they do not sell, but because they cannot properly manage the money that comes in.

According to Dornelas (2022), financial control allows the entrepreneur to make strategic decisions, reduce waste and have the predictability needed to grow.

Cash flow helps answer important questions:

– How much is my company really profiting?

– Am I charging enough?

– Can I invest right now?

– Am I mixing my personal money with the company's?

As Chiavenato (2021) states, “what is not controlled cannot be improved”.

Practical tip:

Even without hiring an accountant at the start, simple spreadsheets or finance apps can help with daily tracking.

2. Pricing: Charging the Right Price Is Surviving

One of the most common mistakes among small entrepreneurs is setting prices based on the competition or on guesswork.

Many charge only to “avoid losing the customer”, without calculating costs, time invested, materials, taxes, travel and profit margin.

According to Kotler and Keller (2019), pricing should take three main factors into account:

Costs

How much it costs to produce or deliver the service.

Perceived value

How much value the customer perceives in what you offer.

Positioning strategy

What image your brand wants to convey to the market.

When the price is badly calculated, the entrepreneur can work very hard and still make no profit.

As Sebrae (2023) highlights, financially sustainable companies need a clear pricing policy.

More information in this article with our dear Sonia

https://tdcriativo.wixsite.com/brasileirosnairlanda/post/gest%C3%A3o-financeira-o-alicerce-invis%C3%ADvel-de-todo-neg%C3%B3cio-que-prospera

3. Sales Strategy: Those Who Never Learn to Sell Will Struggle

Selling does not mean insisting or pressuring people.

In fact, selling means understanding needs and offering solutions.

Daniel Pink (2013) argues that, in today's world, we are all salespeople in some way — including entrepreneurs.

A good sales strategy involves:

Attract

Showing your product or service to the right people.

Talk

Understanding the customer's pain points and needs.

Close

Presenting solutions and making the buying decision easier.

Companies that invest in relationships with customers tend to sell more and build authority.

4. Getting Paid: Professionalism Also Means Knowing How to Charge

Many small entrepreneurs feel embarrassed or uncomfortable about asking clients to pay.

However, getting paid is part of running a business.

According to Robbins and Coulter (2020), organised processes reduce conflict and strengthen the professional image of the business.

Having contracts, defined deadlines, organised messages and clear communication prevents future friction.

Asking to be paid is not rude.

Asking to be paid is respecting your own work.

5. Purchasing and Stock Control

Buying too much can lead to waste. Buying too little can lead to lost sales.

Balance is essential.

According to Slack and Brandon-Jones (2022), good stock management reduces operating costs and improves the company's efficiency.

The entrepreneur needs to learn:

– How much to buy

– When to buy

– Which supplier offers the best value for money

– What actually sells

Being organised in this area prevents money from sitting idle and increases profitability.

6. Marketing and Social Media: Your Business Needs to Be Seen

Today, many companies have their main shop window on social media.

However, posting at random does not mean doing marketing.

Kotler, Kartajaya and Setiawan (2021) state that modern marketing involves relationships, positioning and building value.

Important questions:

– Does my brand convey trust?

– Does my profile look professional?

– Am I creating content that answers the customer's questions?

Companies that position themselves well on social media achieve greater reach, credibility and sales.

7. Photos of Your Product or Service: First Impressions Matter

On social media, the image sells.

A good photo conveys quality, organisation and professionalism.

According to Solomon (2020), consumers are highly influenced by visual cues during the buying decision process.

You do not need to start with expensive equipment.

But it is important to invest in:

– Good lighting

– A tidy setting

– Sharp images

– Before and after (when applicable)

– A professional visual presentation

Often, the customer buys with their eyes first.

8. Customer Service and After-Sales: Good Customers Come Back

Winning a customer costs more than keeping a satisfied one.

According to Kotler and Keller (2019), building customer loyalty increases profit and strengthens the brand's reputation.

After-sales can include:

– A thank-you message

– A request for feedback

– Promotions for long-standing customers

– Follow-up after the service

Well-served customers do not just come back — they recommend you.

And word of mouth is still one of the most powerful forms of marketing.

9. Organisation and Strategy: Growing Without Direction Is Hard

Companies do not grow through effort alone.

They grow through organisation.

Peter Drucker (2006) stated that efficiency is doing things right; strategy is doing what really matters.

Having goals, planning and vision helps the entrepreneur move out of survival mode.

Small consistent actions generate big results over time.

Conclusion

Being an entrepreneur requires courage, learning and adaptation.

At the start, it is normal to have to take on several roles. That does not mean failure — it means building.

The good news is that nobody has to know everything at once.

The secret is to keep learning, seek training and improve one step at a time.

As Peter Drucker used to say:

“The best way to predict the future is to create it.”

If you are a small entrepreneur, keep learning. Your business's growth begins with the knowledge you decide to acquire today.
